[[Category:Gortin Townland, Derryloran Parish, County Tyrone]]
== Biography ==
John may have been born about 1808 or later.

John lived at Gortin, Derryloran, County Tyrone as of 1874; he was an unmarried farmer and his father was Samuel Glasgow. He may have been the son of [[Glasgow-2054|Samuel Glasgow]] and [[McCormick-8286|Ann McCormick]]. 

On 17 June 1874 at Claggan Presbyterian, he married Mary Jane Jordan of Cluntyganny, daughter of Thomas Jordan, farmer. Witnessed by Robert G. Ramsay and John Crooks.
<ref>[https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/details-civil/d2b3612835714 John Glasgow, Mary Jordan, 1874, Magherafelt] at Irish Civil Registration - Marriages</ref>

He passed away 7 November 1896 at Cluntyganny. Informed by Mary Glasgow, widow.
<ref>[https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/details-civil/f1204a4147810 John Glasgow, 1896, Cookstown, 88] at Irish Civil Registration - Deaths</ref>
A marriage for John Glasgow and Jordan was registered on 7 June 1874 in the Cookstown district.<ref>[https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk/search/marriage GRONI civil marriage index], 7 June 1874, Cookstown district, M/1874/L1/1127/1/89.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
=== Individual father review, 22 October 2026 ===

This dated review supersedes any earlier grade of this pair within the stated record scope. The existing father [[Glasgow-2054]] is assessed at 86% (probable). John’s 1874 marriage names Samuel Glasgow as father and places John at Gortin; succession to Samuel’s farms independently supports this specific family. John’s 1896 age 88 conflicts with the c.1815 working birth and needs checking, but does not erase the named-father evidence.

Selected father-profile identity and paternal relationship; maternal identity is separate.

Next useful test: Read the original 1896 age and 1874 father occupation alongside land succession.

Source basis already held: [https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/details-civil/d2b3612835714 John Glasgow, Mary Jordan, 1874, Magherafelt (https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/details-civil/d2b3612835714) at Irish Civil Registration - Marriages]. No new father attached; cited evidence and any inspected register entry are scoped above.


When [[Glasgow-2054|Samuel Glasgow]] dies, the informant is "John Glasgow" ; and some of Samuel's land at Gortin passes to John Glasgow . The land held by John Glasgow passes to John Baine in 1897.

The marriage record for this John placing him at Gortin , and the 1896 death, indicates that it is probably the same John in that marriage as in the valuation books, i.e. that this John was a close relative of [[Glasgow-2054|Samuel]].

All of this seems to indicate John was Samuel's son; however the "age 88" on the death record is not really compatible with that.   Perhaps the age was mistranscribed on the death record.

Another possibility could be that John was a brother rather than a son; however there seems to be some evidence that Samuel's father was called John and not Samuel.

The death of John Glasgow was registered on 7 November 1896 in Cookstown, aged 88.<ref>[https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk/search/death GRONI civil death index], John Glasgow, 7 November 1896, aged 88, Cookstown registration district, D/1896/99/1009/15/479.</ref>

A possible identification concerns John Glasgow, Drogheda sub-constable, 1850. Sub-constable John Glasgow, explicitly of the Drogheda police, appears in a court report on 19 October 1850. He found the prisoner running away with a bag of meal in an oatmeal-theft case. John is the police witness, not the accused.<ref>The Drogheda Argus and Leinster Journal, 19 October 1850, p.2, court theft report; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/1259561281/ record].</ref> Occupation and police station are explicit; age, birthplace, relatives and exact service dates are unstated. [[Glasgow-2056]], [[Glasgow-2537]] and [[Glasgow-867]] are adult chronology comparisons only, with no checked constabulary connection. An administrative Drogheda probate label on a different John lead is not evidence of Drogheda residence or police service. Royal Irish Constabulary service records and local directories are the next identity tests. The identification remains uncertain.
